[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

Messages that cannot be processed — whether due to invalid payload structure, unrecoverable downstream failures, expired TTL, or queue overflow — must not be silently discarded. Without a dead-letter queue (DLQ), failed messages are lost the moment the broker drops them; failures are invisible to operators; there is no path to recovery, investigation, or replay. In healthcare applications, a silently dropped eligibility event or lost claim task is not just an operational inconvenience — it is a compliance risk.
page_texts.5:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#solution-overview]

### Solution Overview

Configure a Dead Letter Channel (DLC) — a dedicated dead-letter exchange (DLX) and dead-letter queue (DLQ) — on every production queue. When a broker dead-letters a message due to consumer rejection, message TTL expiry, or queue length overflow, the broker automatically routes it to the DLX, which forwards it to the corresponding DLQ. A dedicated DLQ consumer, management UI inspection, or automated replay tooling handles dead-lettered messages. CloudWatch alerts on DLQ depth notify the on-call team when dead letters appear.

Within the enterprise platform, Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ) is the supported broker implementation for this pattern. For all enterprise-mandated configuration requirements — DLX/DLQ naming conventions, `x-dead-letter-exchange` queue argument requirements, TLS, credential management — refer to [STD-APP-EVT-007 — RabbitMQ Enterprise Messaging Standard](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#when-to-use]

### When to Use

- **All Production Queues**: Every durable production queue where message loss would have unacceptable business or compliance impact should have a Dead Letter Channel configured. Enterprise requirements are defined in STD-APP-EVT-007.
- **Work Queues (PTN-APP-EVT-016)**: The primary source of consumer-rejected dead letters from task processing failures
- **Request Queues (PTN-APP-EVT-018)**: Requests that responders cannot process (schema validation failure, permanent downstream error) must be dead-lettered rather than silently dropped
- **Pub-Sub Subscriber Queues (PTN-APP-EVT-017)**: Each subscriber queue should have its own DLQ; subscriber failures must not block other subscribers or drop events

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#when-not-to-use]

### When NOT to Use

This pattern is strongly recommended for all production queues in healthcare and human services systems. Exceptions (e.g., ephemeral scratch queues used only in development) should be documented and reviewed. Enterprise mandatory requirements are specified in STD-APP-EVT-007.

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#benefits]

### Benefits

- **Message Durability on Failure**: Dead-lettered messages are not lost; they are preserved in the DLQ for investigation and replay
- **Operational Visibility**: DLQ depth is a clear, actionable signal — a non-zero DLQ means something is failing and requires attention
- **Failure Isolation**: Dead letters in the DLQ do not block the source queue or other consumers; the source queue continues to process healthy messages
- **Recovery Path**: DLQ messages can be inspected, fixed, and replayed to the source queue without re-submitting from the original producer
- **Compliance Audit Trail**: The `x-death` header appended by the broker provides a structured audit record of every dead-letter event (reason, timestamp, count, source queue)
- **HIPAA Risk Mitigation**: Lost eligibility events and dropped claim tasks represent compliance risk; DLQ prevents silent message loss

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#business-context]

### Business Context

Healthcare and human services applications process messages that represent high-value business operations: eligibility determinations, claim adjudications, payment events, document ingestion, case updates. Each of these operations has real-world consequences if it is silently skipped. Examples of failures that generate dead letters:

- **Claim Adjudication Task Failure**: A claim task fails schema validation (missing required field introduced by a producer bug). Without a DLQ, the task is dropped; the claim is never adjudicated; the provider never receives payment authorisation.
- **Eligibility Event Processing Failure**: A downstream database is temporarily unavailable; the subscriber NACKs after retry exhaustion. Without a DLQ, the eligibility event is lost; a member's record is never updated; they are denied benefits they are entitled to.
- **Document Processing Timeout**: An OCR processing task exceeds TTL configured on the queue. Without a DLQ, the document is dropped; the prior authorisation request is incomplete; clinical workflow is blocked.

Business requirements include:

- **Zero Silent Message Loss**: Every message that cannot be processed must be preserved for investigation and recovery
- **Alerting on Failures**: Operations teams must be notified when dead letters occur so they can investigate root cause and initiate recovery
- **Replay Without Re-Submission**: Dead-lettered messages must be replayable from the DLQ without requiring the original producer to re-submit — the producer may no longer have the data, or re-submission may cause duplicates at the producer level

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

The enterprise platform uses Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ) as the message broker. Most modern message brokers support some form of dead-letter routing (RabbitMQ via `x-dead-letter-exchange` queue arguments, Amazon SQS via Dead Letter Queues, Azure Service Bus via dead-lettering properties). The pattern described here is conceptually portable; enterprise-specific queue argument names, naming conventions, and constraints are defined in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

Dead-lettering is performed by the broker — no application code is required to route messages to the DLQ once the topology is configured correctly.

**How RabbitMQ Dead-Letters a Message:**

RabbitMQ automatically routes a message to the DLX (and thus the DLQ) when any of the following conditions occur:

1. **Consumer NACK with `requeue=False`**: A consumer calls `basic_nack(requeue=False)` or `basic_reject(requeue=False)`, explicitly declining to process the message and requesting it not be re-enqueued
2. **Message TTL Expiry**: A message has been waiting in the queue longer than the `x-message-ttl` queue argument value
3. **Queue Length Overflow**: The queue has reached its `x-max-length` or `x-max-length-bytes` limit; the oldest (or newest, depending on overflow policy) messages are dead-lettered to make room

**Current State Without DLQ:**

- Messages dead-lettered by the broker without a configured DLX are silently dropped
- No visibility into failure rate or failure reason; operators have no signal
- No recovery path; permanently failed messages are gone
- Compliance audit trail is incomplete; there is no record of dropped messages
- Teams implement inconsistent ad-hoc workarounds (logging to a database, catching NACKs at the application layer) that are not standardised or monitored uniformly

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#problem-details]

### Problem Details

**Problem 1: Silent Message Loss**

Without a DLX, any message the broker would dead-letter simply disappears. The producer believes the message was delivered; the consumer declined to process it; the broker drops it. No log entry at the broker level; no metric spike; no alert. The failure is discovered only when a downstream system shows missing data — often hours or days later.

**Problem 2: No Structured Failure Metadata**

Even when applications log failures, the failure context is in application logs and not associated with the message. The broker's `x-death` header — which records reason, timestamp, source queue, exchange, routing keys, and retry count — is only available when DLQ is configured. Without it, post-incident analysis must reconstruct the failure timeline from application logs, which are often incomplete or inconsistent.

**Problem 3: No Standardised Recovery Path**

Without a DLQ, recovery requires the original producer to re-submit the message. For batch-ingested data, the producer may need to re-run a batch job; for real-time events, the producer may have already discarded the source record. With a DLQ, the message is preserved with its original payload and headers; replay requires only routing the DLQ message back to the source queue.

**Problem 4: Poison Message Loops**

When a consumer NACKs with `requeue=True`, the message is immediately re-enqueued and redelivered. If the failure is permanent (e.g., malformed payload the consumer can never process), the message is redelivered in a tight loop, consuming 100% of one consumer's capacity while preventing other messages from being processed. DLQ with a retry limit (tracked via `x-death` count) breaks this loop by routing the poison message out of the source queue after a maximum number of attempts.

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#forces-and-constraints]

### Forces and Constraints

- **PHI Sensitivity**: DLQ messages may contain PHI subject to the same data governance and access controls as the source queue. Mandatory requirements for PHI handling in dead-letter channels are defined in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).
- **Managed Broker Constraints**: When using Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ), certain topology arguments such as `x-dead-letter-exchange` must be declared as queue arguments rather than policy arguments. Specific constraints are detailed in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).
- **Broker Isolation**: Dead letter exchanges and queues must reside in the same broker vhost or namespace as the source queue. Cross-namespace routing is not supported.
- **Monitoring**: Broker metrics for queue depth are the primary indicator for DLQ health. Enterprise monitoring integration (CloudWatch, RabbitMQ Management API) details are specified in STD-APP-EVT-007.

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#pattern-description]

### Pattern Description

The Dead-Letter Handling pattern is built on three tiers:

**Tier 1: DLQ Configuration (Automatic Broker Routing)**

Every production source queue declares two arguments:

- `x-dead-letter-exchange`: The name of the DLX (a separate direct exchange dedicated to dead-letter routing for this domain). When the broker dead-letters a message from this queue, it publishes it to this exchange.
- `x-dead-letter-routing-key` (optional but recommended): The routing key used when publishing to the DLX. If omitted, the original routing key is used. Setting this explicitly to the source queue name makes DLQ topology unambiguous and inspectable.

A DLQ (a separate durable queue) is bound to the DLX with a routing key matching the dead-letter routing key. Dead-lettered messages arrive at the DLQ with their original headers intact plus an appended `x-death` array header containing per-dead-letter metadata.

**Tier 2: DLQ Monitoring (Visibility and Alerting)**

DLQ depth is monitored continuously. A CloudWatch alert fires when DLQ depth exceeds a configurable threshold (default: 0 — any dead-lettered message warrants investigation). Alert thresholds and on-call routing are pending configuration per team and per domain SLA.

**Tier 3: DLQ Consumer Strategies (Recovery)**

Three strategies are available depending on use case:

1. **Manual Inspection**: DLQ messages are inspected via RabbitMQ Management UI or a custom inspection tool; the operator determines whether to replay (republish to source queue) or discard after root cause resolution.
2. **Automated Delayed Retry**: A DLQ consumer republishes messages to the source queue after a configurable delay. Uses a "retry queue" with per-message TTL to implement delay without the `rabbitmq-delayed-message-exchange` plugin (which may not be available on Amazon MQ).
3. **Parking Lot / Audit Archive**: A DLQ consumer persists the message body and headers to a database or S3 bucket for long-term audit retention before acknowledging and removing from the DLQ. Required for HIPAA compliance contexts where dead-lettered messages contain PHI.

**Key Design Decisions:**

- DLQ is separate per source queue — a shared DLQ makes it impossible to identify which workflow produced a failure
- DLQ itself does not have a DLX — dead letters from the DLQ are not re-dead-lettered; they must be explicitly acked or nacked by the DLQ consumer
- `x-message-ttl` on the source queue prevents poison messages from waiting indefinitely (also triggers dead-lettering on TTL expiry)
- `x-death` header is preserved through the DLQ and must be included in archived records

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#components]

### Components

| Component | Responsibility | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Source Queue** | Primary processing queue; configured with `x-dead-letter-exchange` | Durable; TTL and max-length set per domain SLA |
| **DLX Exchange** | Routes dead-lettered messages to the DLQ | Direct exchange; one per domain or per source queue |
| **DLQ** | Holds dead-lettered messages for investigation, replay, or archival | Durable; no `x-dead-letter-exchange` on the DLQ itself |
| **DLQ Consumer** | Inspects `x-death` headers; archives, replays, or discards messages | Automated or operator-driven; must not loop messages back indefinitely |
| **CloudWatch Alert** | Fires when DLQ depth > configured threshold | Threshold: 0 (investigate any dead letter) or calibrated per team SLA |
| **Audit Archive** | Persists dead-lettered message body and headers for HIPAA retention | Required when source queue may contain PHI |

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#interactions]

### Interactions

**NACK → Dead-Letter Path:**

1. Consumer receives message from source queue
2. Consumer determines the failure is permanent (schema validation error, max retries exceeded)
3. Consumer calls `basic_nack(delivery_tag=..., requeue=False)`
4. RabbitMQ routes message to DLX exchange with `x-dead-letter-routing-key`
5. DLX exchange forwards to DLQ with `x-death` header appended
6. CloudWatch DLQ depth metric increments; alert fires if depth > threshold
7. DLQ consumer picks up message; inspects `x-death.reason`; archives and/or replays

**TTL Expiry → Dead-Letter Path:**

1. Message arrives in source queue but no consumer is available (all consumers down or overloaded)
2. Message waits in queue beyond `x-message-ttl` value
3. RabbitMQ dead-letters the message with `x-death.reason=expired`
4. Same flow as NACK path from step 4 onward

**Replay Path:**

1. Operator or DLQ consumer determines dead-lettered message can be reprocessed (root cause fixed)
2. Message is republished to source queue (via default exchange or original exchange with original routing key)
3. Source queue consumer reprocesses; ACKs on success
4. DLQ message is acknowledged and removed from DLQ

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#variations]

### Variations

**Variation 1: Delayed Retry via Retry Queue**

Instead of replaying directly to the source queue, route dead-lettered messages to a "retry queue" with a fixed TTL. When the TTL expires, the retry queue dead-letters its messages back to the source queue (the retry queue's `x-dead-letter-exchange` points to the original exchange). This implements a delay without requiring the `rabbitmq-delayed-message-exchange` plugin.

**Variation 2: Exponential Backoff with Multiple Retry Queues**

Declare multiple retry queues with increasing TTLs (e.g., 10s, 60s, 300s). The DLQ consumer inspects the `x-death.count` header and routes to the appropriate retry queue based on attempt number. After the maximum attempt count, the message is routed to a "parking lot" queue for manual investigation.

**Variation 3: Consumer-Side Failure-Type Routing**

The `x-dead-letter-exchange` is a queue-level argument and cannot be overridden on a per-message basis in AMQP 0-9-1 or RabbitMQ. The `CC` header is a carbon copy routing mechanism at **publish time** and does not affect dead-letter routing.

To route different failure types to different destinations, use consumer-side logic:

- **Multiple source queues**: Declare separate source queues, each with a different `x-dead-letter-exchange`, and publish messages to the appropriate queue based on message type or priority.
- **Consumer-side publish-on-failure**: Rather than relying on broker-level dead-lettering for all failure types, the consumer code ACKs the message and explicitly publishes to the appropriate DLQ or error queue based on the exception type. This requires careful handling to ensure the ACK and publish are consistent.

**Variation 4: DLQ Consumer with Circuit Breaker**

A DLQ consumer that attempts automated replay implements a circuit breaker: if replay success rate drops below a threshold (indicating the source queue consumers are still failing), the circuit opens and stops replaying. This prevents a replay storm from overwhelming a recovering consumer pool.

### Prerequisites

**Infrastructure Requirements:**

- Amazon MQ (RabbitMQ 3.11+) instance accessible from application namespaces
- Virtual host provisioned for the domain — pending discovery of vhost provisioning process with Platform Engineering
- TLS-enabled AMQP endpoint (`amqps://` — port 5671)
- IAM or Secrets Manager credentials for broker authentication
- CloudWatch integration for queue depth monitoring via Amazon MQ CloudWatch integration (confirm metric availability with Platform Engineering)
- S3 bucket or database for DLQ message archival (if PHI payloads require HIPAA-compliant long-term retention)

**Technical Skills:**

- Understanding of dead-letter exchange mechanics and failure header structure (`x-death` on RabbitMQ; equivalent on other brokers)
- Familiarity with message TTL, queue length limits, and overflow semantics
- Experience with structured error handling and idempotent retry logic

**Organizational Readiness:**

- Naming convention agreement per STD-APP-EVT-007 for DLX and DLQ naming
- DLQ monitoring alert routing and on-call runbook per domain team
- Defined per-queue retry limits and TTL values (pending discovery with domain owners)
- Defined retention policy for archived DLQ messages

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#conceptual-implementation-steps]

#### Conceptual Implementation Steps

At a pattern level, the implementation sequence is:

1. **Declare the Dead Letter Exchange (DLX)**: A durable direct exchange dedicated to dead-letter routing for the domain — idempotent, declared at startup
2. **Declare the Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)**: A durable queue bound to the DLX with a routing key matching the source queue name — do NOT add a DLX to the DLQ itself (avoids infinite loops)
3. **Declare the source queue with dead-letter routing**: Set `x-dead-letter-exchange` (and optionally `x-dead-letter-routing-key`) as queue arguments; add `x-message-ttl` per domain SLA
4. **Consumer: reject unrecoverable messages explicitly**: Call NACK (or equivalent) with `requeue=False` for permanent failures or after max retry exhaustion; track retry attempts using a custom application header (`x-retry-count`) incremented on each republish — do NOT rely on `x-death.count` with `requeue=True` as `x-death` is only populated on dead-lettering, not on requeue; use `requeue=True` only for single-attempt transient failures with no retry counting requirement
5. **DLQ Consumer: inspect, archive, optionally replay**: Read `x-death` headers (reason, count, source queue, timestamp); archive to audit store if PHI is present; replay to source queue after root cause resolution; enforce a max replay limit
6. **Monitor DLQ depth**: Alert when DLQ depth exceeds configured threshold (default: any non-zero reading warrants investigation)

All naming conventions, specific argument values, TTL defaults, and technology-specific configuration are defined in [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

> **For the complete RabbitMQ implementation example** including full topology setup, DLQ consumer, delayed retry pattern, and archival integration — see [STD-APP-EVT-007 — RabbitMQ Enterprise Messaging Standard](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#best-practices]

### Best Practices

1. **Declare DLQ Topology Before Source Queue**: Declare the dead-letter exchange and DLQ before declaring the source queue. If the source queue is declared first referencing a dead-letter exchange that does not yet exist, messages that should be routed to dead-letter are dropped rather than captured.

2. **Never Add a Dead-Letter Route to the DLQ Itself**: The DLQ must not have its own dead-letter exchange configured. If a DLQ consumer rejects a DLQ message without a fallback route, the message is dropped, which is the correct behaviour. A DLX on the DLQ creates an infinite loop.

3. **Log Failure Metadata on Every DLQ Message**: The broker-appended failure metadata header (`x-death` on RabbitMQ) is the primary diagnostic artifact for post-incident analysis. Every DLQ consumer must log the failure reason, count, source queue, and timestamp alongside the message's `correlation_id` and `message_id`.

4. **Preserve `correlation_id` and `message_id` Through Replay**: When replaying a dead-lettered message to the source queue, preserve the original `correlation_id` and `message_id` from the dead-lettered message properties. This maintains the audit trail and enables idempotent processing checks in the source consumer.

5. **Set TTL on Source Queues, Not DLQs (by default)**: TTL on DLQ messages prevents the DLQ from growing unbounded but also permanently destroys unprocessed dead letters after the TTL window. Only add TTL to the DLQ if the domain team has explicitly defined a retention window and accepted the risk of permanent loss after expiry.

6. **Monitor DLQ Depth Continuously**: DLQ depth should be treated as a health indicator equivalent to a 5xx error rate. A sustained non-zero DLQ depth signals systematic failures. Integrate DLQ depth alerts into your team's on-call rotation.

7. **Separate DLQ per Source Queue**: A shared DLQ (one DLQ for multiple source queues) makes it impossible to quickly identify which workflow is failing. The operational overhead of per-queue DLQs is minimal and justified by the clarity of isolated failure signals.

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

1. **Dead-Letter Routing Key Mismatch**: Some brokers use the original routing key of the dead-lettered message if no explicit dead-letter routing key is configured. If the DLQ binding uses a different key, dead letters are silently dropped. Always configure the dead-letter routing key explicitly and verify the DLQ binding matches.

2. **Declaring Source Queue Before Dead-Letter Topology**: If the source queue references a dead-letter exchange that does not yet exist, dead-lettered messages are dropped. Always declare the dead-letter exchange and DLQ before the source queue.

3. **Infinite Retry Loop on DLQ**: A DLQ consumer that unconditionally republishes to the source queue without checking the broker-appended retry count creates an infinite retry loop for permanently failing messages. Always inspect the failure count header and enforce a maximum replay limit.

4. **PHI in Dead-Letter Archives Without Access Controls**: DLQ messages may contain PHI. If dead-letter archives are written to a database or object store, the same access controls (IAM policies, encryption at rest, audit logging) required for the source queue must apply to the archive. Do not write dead-letter archives to uncontrolled storage.

5. **Requeue Without Retry Limit**: Using NACK with `requeue=True` (or equivalent) without tracking retry count creates a poison message loop. The message is redelivered immediately and repeatedly, consuming all consumer capacity. Always track delivery count and route to dead-letter after a configurable retry budget is exhausted.

6. **Auto-Acknowledge on DLQ Consumer**: If the DLQ consumer uses automatic acknowledgement and crashes during archival, the dead-lettered message is permanently lost. Always use manual acknowledgement on DLQ consumers; acknowledge only after successful archival or an explicit discard decision.

page_texts.28:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#compliance-requirements]

### Compliance Requirements

All mandatory compliance requirements for this pattern — TLS connection rules, PHI access controls for DLQ queues and archives, dead-letter archive retention periods, and operational alerting thresholds — are defined in:

**[STD-APP-EVT-007 — RabbitMQ Enterprise Messaging Standard](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md)**

Pattern-level guidance:

- **PHI Sensitivity**: DLQ queues and dead-letter archives may contain PHI from the source queue. The same access controls, encryption at rest, and audit logging requirements that apply to the source queue apply to the DLQ and its archive.
- **Audit Trail**: Broker-appended failure metadata (e.g., `x-death` on RabbitMQ) provides a structured audit record of each dead-letter event. These records must be preserved per applicable retention policies when the dead-lettered message contained PHI.
- **PHI in Message Properties**: PHI must not appear in queue names, exchange names, routing keys, or monitoring metric dimensions.
- **DLQ Resolution SLA**: DLQ messages must not accumulate indefinitely; each team must define and enforce a review SLA for dead-lettered messages.

### Monitoring and Metrics

| Metric | Target | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **DLQ Depth (`messages_ready`)** | 0 (any value triggers investigation) | Amazon MQ CloudWatch / RabbitMQ Management API |
| **DLQ Message Rate (ingress)** | 0 baseline; non-zero warrants investigation | Amazon MQ CloudWatch |

**Alerting Thresholds (pending calibration with domain owners):**

- **Critical**: DLQ depth > 10 messages; source queue consumer count = 0 for > 2 minutes
- **Warning**: DLQ depth > 0; DLQ ingress rate > 1 message/minute sustained for 5 minutes
- **Info**: Single DLQ message detected; DLQ message archived successfully

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#example-1-claim-adjudication-task--schema-validation-failure]

### Example 1: Claim Adjudication Task — Schema Validation Failure

**Context:** A producer bug introduces a new required field (`claimVersion`) in claim adjudication task payloads but omits it from 300 messages published before the fix is deployed. The adjudication worker performs schema validation on every message and NACKs with `requeue=False` for schema failures.

**Topology:**

- Source Queue: `claims.adjudication.tasks` (durable, `x-dead-letter-exchange=claims.tasks.dlx`, `x-message-ttl=86400000`)
- DLQ: `claims.adjudication.tasks.dlq`
- DLQ Consumer: inspects `x-death.reason`; archives to DynamoDB with full payload and headers

**Flow:**

1. 300 malformed messages are NACKed with `requeue=False`; broker routes to DLX → DLQ
2. CloudWatch alert fires: DLQ depth > 0
3. On-call team investigates; identifies missing `claimVersion` field; rolls back producer
4. DLQ consumer has archived all 300 messages with original payloads
5. Team deploys fixed producer; replays 300 archived messages to `claims.adjudication.tasks`
6. All 300 tasks processed successfully; DLQ depth returns to 0
page_texts.33:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#example-2-eligibility-event-subscriber--delayed-retry-after-database-failure]

### Example 2: Eligibility Event Subscriber — Delayed Retry After Database Failure

**Context:** A downstream database becomes temporarily unavailable for 4 minutes during a maintenance window. An eligibility event subscriber NACKs after 3 retry attempts, routing 85 events to the DLQ.

**Flow:**

1. 85 eligibility events dead-lettered during the 4-minute database outage
2. DLQ consumer detects `x-death.reason=rejected` and `x-death.count <= 5`
3. DLQ consumer republishes to `eligibility.events.retry` queue (60-second TTL)
4. After 60 seconds, retry queue TTL expires; messages dead-letter back to the source queue via default exchange
5. Source queue consumer (now with restored database connectivity) processes all 85 messages successfully
6. DLQ depth returns to 0; alert clears
page_texts.34:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#example-3-document-processing-task--ttl-expiry-during-consumer-outage]

### Example 3: Document Processing Task — TTL Expiry During Consumer Outage

**Context:** All document processing worker pods are inadvertently deleted during a Kubernetes deployment rollback. 42 document processing tasks accumulate in the queue for 25 hours, exceeding the 24-hour `x-message-ttl` value.

**Flow:**

1. 42 tasks expire in the source queue after 24 hours; broker dead-letters with `x-death.reason=expired`
2. CloudWatch alert: DLQ depth > 0 (also: Consumer count = 0 has been alerting for 25 hours)
3. On-call team redeploys workers; investigates DLQ
4. `x-death.reason=expired` signals TTL expiry, not processing failure — payloads are valid
5. Operator replays all 42 DLQ messages to source queue; workers process successfully
6. Post-incident review: add Consumer count = 0 alert with shorter detection window (2 minutes)
page_texts.36:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#scenario-1-poison-message-isolation]

#### Scenario 1: Poison Message Isolation

A malformed message (corrupted binary payload) causes a worker to crash on every attempt. Without a retry limit and DLQ, this message would be redelivered in a tight loop, preventing all other tasks in the queue from being processed. With `MAX_RETRIES=3` and NACK on exhaustion, the message is routed to the DLQ after 3 attempts. The remaining 1,000 valid tasks in the queue are processed normally. The on-call team investigates the dead-lettered message and identifies the corruption source.
page_texts.37:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#scenario-2-bulk-replay-after-root-cause-resolution]

#### Scenario 2: Bulk Replay After Root Cause Resolution

A rules engine upgrade introduces a breaking change in the response schema, causing 500 adjudication tasks to fail and dead-letter over 2 hours. After the rules engine is rolled back and the consumer is patched, an operator uses the RabbitMQ Management UI (or a custom replay script) to republish all 500 DLQ messages to the source queue. All 500 tasks are processed within 15 minutes. No data is re-submitted from the original producer; no duplicates are created at the submission layer.
page_texts.38:
[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#scenario-3-compliance-audit-of-dead-lettered-phi]

#### Scenario 3: Compliance Audit of Dead-Lettered PHI

A HIPAA audit requires demonstration that PHI contained in dead-lettered messages was not exposed. The DLQ consumer's archive records — stored in an encrypted DynamoDB table with IAM-controlled access — show: which messages were dead-lettered, when, from which queue, for what reason, and that access to the archive was limited to two authorised operations personnel over the audit period. The audit is satisfied without requiring raw broker log analysis.

[patterns/application/event-driven/PTN-APP-EVT-019-messaging-dead-letter-channel-pattern.md#tldr]

## TL;DR

**Problem:** Messages that cannot be processed (invalid payload, permanent downstream failure, TTL expiry, queue overflow) are silently dropped by RabbitMQ if no dead-letter exchange is configured. In healthcare applications, this means lost eligibility events, dropped claim tasks, and compliance audit gaps — with no operational signal and no recovery path.

**Solution:** Configure a Dead Letter Channel — a dedicated dead-letter exchange (DLX) and dead-letter queue (DLQ) — on every production queue. Failed or expired messages are automatically routed by the broker to the DLQ; no application code required. A DLQ consumer inspects broker-appended failure metadata, archives messages for compliance, and optionally replays them to the source queue after root cause resolution. Enterprise implementation uses Amazon MQ (managed RabbitMQ) per [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md).

**When to Use:**

- All production queues where silent message loss would have unacceptable business or compliance impact
- Work queues (primary source of consumer-rejected dead letters)
- Request queues (unprocessable requests)
- Pub-sub subscriber queues (subscriber failure isolation)

**Key Benefits:**

- Zero silent message loss — every dead-lettered message is preserved in the DLQ
- Broker-appended failure metadata (`x-death` on RabbitMQ) provides a structured audit trail per dead-letter event
- DLQ isolation prevents failing messages from blocking the source queue
- Replay path enables recovery without re-submission from the original producer
- PHI-containing dead-lettered messages can be archived with full compliance controls

**Implementation Complexity:** Low (topology configuration) to Medium (DLQ consumer with archival and delayed retry)

**Prerequisites:** Amazon MQ (RabbitMQ) instance, vhost provisioned per domain, TLS-enabled AMQP endpoint, CloudWatch DLQ depth alerting, archive storage target for PHI retention (pending team-specific discovery)

**Related Patterns:** [PTN-APP-EVT-016 (Work Queue)](./PTN-APP-EVT-016-messaging-work-queue-pattern.md), [PTN-APP-EVT-017 (Publish-Subscribe)](./PTN-APP-EVT-017-messaging-publish-subscribe-pattern.md), [PTN-APP-EVT-018 (Request-Reply)](./PTN-APP-EVT-018-messaging-request-reply-pattern.md), [PTN-INFRA-EVT-001 (DLQ Pattern)](../../infrastructure/event-driven/PTN-INFRA-EVT-001-infrastructure-dead-letter-queue-pattern.md), [STD-APP-EVT-007](../../../standards/application/event-driven/STD-APP-EVT-007-rabbitmq-enterprise-messaging-standard.md)
